A 60-year-old gentleman presents with a two week history of fever (38.5°C on admission). He describes a two week history of weakness andnight sweats.
On initial examination he had an early diastolic murmur. Three sets of blood culture grew S. bovis. He successfully completes treatment forinfective endocarditis. Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiograms had both demonstrated vegetations on the aortic valve but noaortic root abscess.
Which of the following investigations would be most appropriate to organise before discharge?
explanation:
This gentleman requires gastrointestinal (GI) investigations as S. bovis bacteraemia infective endocarditis is strongly associated withGI malignancy. He is most likely to be suffering from infective endocarditis rather than another cause.
The portal of entry of S.bovis is the gastrointestinal tract. Rarely, the urinary tract, the hepatobiliary tree or oropharynx have beenreported as the source of the bacteraemia.
There is a strong association between S. bovis bacteraemia with or without endocarditis and malignancy or premalignancy withinthe colon.
Patients with S. bovis bacteraemia should be investigated for a GI malignancy.
Reference:1. Murray HW, Roberts RB. Streptococcus bovis bacteremia and underlying gastrointestinal disease. Arch Intern Med.1978;138:1097-9.2. UpToDate. Microbiology, pathogenesis, and epidemiology of Streptococcus bovis infection.

His chest x ray is unremarkable and his ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no other abnormality seen. He is a heavy smoker and has been onholiday to Florida recently. He is tachycardic and his respiratory rate is 32 breaths per minute.
Which is the best investigation to do next?
explanation:
The question suggests that he is tachycardic and tachyapneic with a normal chest x ray after a recent long journey.
A pulmonary embolus needs to be excluded therefore D-dimers is important.
Some credit could be given to CRP in case of infection without initial radiographic features.
Troponin, creatinine kinase and brain natriuretic peptide are not useful.

A 75-year-old man was referred to clinic urgently by his GP because of worsening breathlessness.
The patient had noticed increasing exertional dyspnoea for approximately three months. Before the onset of his symptoms, his exercisecapacity had been unrestricted and he regularly played a round of golf once or twice a week. By the time of his review in clinic, he wasbreathless getting onto the examination couch. He also reported two recent episodes of severe dizziness when he had tried to rush whiledoing the shopping. He did not collapse on either occasion, but felt light-headed and had to sit down. On both occasions he felt as though hewas going to faint.
On examination he was comfortable at rest. His pulse was 90 beats per minute and regular. A parasternal thrill was palpable over the chestwall. A loud ejection systolic murmur was audible in the second right intercostal space and radiated up into the carotid arteries.
A transthoracic echocardiogram showed a peak aortic valve gradient of 100 mmHg with normal left ventricular systolic function. There wereno other valvular abnormalities.
What treatment is next indicated for this gentleman?
explanation:
This patient has developed symptomatic aortic stenosis with a peak gradient of 100 mg with preserved LV systolic function andsymptoms of exertional breathlessness and exercise-induced presyncope.
An aortic valve replacement is prognostically and symptomatically the best treatment option in an older person who can undergothe surgery.
Valvuloplasty is appopriate for younger adults or children with congenital heart disease. It may used for older patients who are notable to undergo surgery.

stem: According to NICE guidelines, what should the initial management be for patients with previous myocardial infarction who have suspectedheart failure?
options: Echocardiography and specialist review within six weeks
Echocardiography and specialist review within two weeks
Treat with furosemide and investigate if no improvement
explanation:
The NICE guidelines recommend that patients with previous myocardial infarction who have suspected heart failure should bereferred for an echocardiogram and specialist review within two weeks.
Patients who do not have a history of infarction, but who have suspected heart failure, should be risk stratiﬁed using serumnatriuretic peptides, such as BNP.
Patients with raised and high BNP concentrations should be referred for echo and specialist review within six weeks and two weeksrespectively.
Patients with normal BNP concentrations should be investigated for other causes of their symptoms as a normal BNP makes heartfailure unlikely.
BNP is also raised in the following:HypertensionAtrial ﬁbrillation (AF)Aortic stenosisDiastolic dysfunctionAcute coronary syndromesCor pulmonale, andStable angina
It is therefore a marker of structural heart disease rather than speciﬁcally a marker of systolic dysfunction.
Elevated BNP is also seen in:Acute and chronic renal failureLiver cirrhosis

A 70-year-old man with a history of alcohol excess, hypertension and smoking presents to you as a follow up in the heart failure clinic.
On grading his symptoms, he appears to be a New York Heart Association (NYHA) grade III. His ECG shows a left bundle branch block (QRS>120 ms) and a recent echocardiogram conﬁrms an ejection fraction of <35%. He is presently on furosemide 80 mg BD, spironolactone 25mg OD, and aspirin 75 mg OD.
What would you consider to be a deﬁnitive management for this man?
explanation:
Cardiac resynchronisation therapy (CRT) is recommended in patients withadvanced HF (usually NYHA class III or IV)severe systolic dysfunction (e.g. left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] ≤ 35%)intraventricular conduction delay (e.g. QRS >120 ms).
The rationale for CRT is that ventricular dyssynchrony can further impair the pump function of a failing ventricle.
Resynchronisation may improve pump performance and reverse the deleterious process of ventricular remodelling.

A 53-year-old man presented to the Emergency department with severe central chest pain.
The 12-lead ECG showed inferior ST segment elevation and he was diagnosed as having an acute inferior myocardial infarction. Thrombolysiswas initiated on the basis of the ECG ﬁndings.
Thirty minutes later in the coronary care unit he developed complete atrial and ventricular dissociation, although he remainedhaemodynamically stable with the blood pressure recorded as 120/80 mmHg. After a further ten minutes he developed intermittent runs ofventricular tachycardia (VT) which were associated with a signiﬁcant fall in the blood pressure to 85/65 mmHg.
Over the subsequent ten minutes his blood pressure stabilised (110/75 mmHg) and no further episodes of ventricular tachycardia wererecorded.
What is his best immediate management?
explanation:
The insertion of a temporary wire in this situation is unnecessary as the patient is haemodynamically stable (now) with completeheart block.
He has had reperfusion arrhythmias (VT), so amiodarone infusion is not required and observation under close ECG monitoring is thebest immediate management.
The use of inotropes in the context of preserved blood pressure is unnecessary and proarrhythmic.
Intravenous aminophylline is useful in complete heart block, as the heart block is often mediated by adenosine which aminophyllineinhibits, however in this context with recent VT with instability this is inappropriate.

A 57-year-old man is recovering on the cardiology ward after suffering an anterior myocardial infarction when he suddenly deteriorates onday four.
When you review him, his BP is 80/60 mmHg, his pulse is 100 and regular, he looks grey and clammy. There is a harsh systolic murmur over awide area including the apex and left sternal edge. There are extensive crackles on auscultation of the chest consistent with pulmonaryoedema.
Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
This patient has suffered a catastrophic event, the clinical picture ﬁtting best with cardiogenic shock secondary to acute ventricularseptal defect. Crucial to prognosis is haemodynamic stabilisation, and in this case with hypotension and shock, IABCP to supportcardiac output is the best approach.
Inotropes such as adrenaline and noradrenaline can signiﬁcantly increase myocardial ischaemia, as such they would only beadjunctive support after IABCP.
Whilst vasodilators such as GTN can signiﬁcantly improve myocardial blood ﬂow, they are inappropriate here because ofhypotension.
Similarly, furosemide alone is unlikely to be suﬃcient

A 70-year-old lady presented with an episode of syncope. Her ECG is shown.
Which of the following best describes the site of the lesion in this lady?
explanation:
The ECG shows 'trifascicular block' which is not strictly an ECG diagnosis but is a term used for the combination of right bundlebranch block, left hemiblock (typically left anterior hemiblock) and long PR interval.
It implies that the bundle branches (Purkinje ﬁbres) are blocked in the right bundle and one of the left hemibundles. The 'third'bundle is also delayed or partially blocked hence the name. However, the delay (long PR interval) is usually at the AV node.
Clinically it means there is extensive disease of the conduction system and, in a patient such as this, would be an indication forpermanent pacemaker.

A 37-year-old lady is brought to the Emergency department with rapidly increasing breathlessness and chest pain over the preceding 48hours.
She had been under the care of rheumatologists for joint symptoms and has been diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).There is no history of recent travel or symptoms to suggest infection.
On examination the patient is short of breath with a respiratory rate of 26. Oxygen saturations are 97% on room air. Pulse is 130 regular andblood pressure is 80/60 mmHg. Cardiac examination is unremarkable but the venous pressure is elevated. There is no peripheral oedema.
A 12 lead ECG reveals a sinus tachycardia only. A chest x ray demonstrates a slightly enlarged heart but clear lung ﬁelds.
Which is the most appropriate next step in this patient's management, from the list below?
options: Full dose low molecular weight heparin
explanation:
This question is diﬃcult.
The case describes a patient with lupus and acute breathlessness. The symptoms and haemodynamic parameters are a worry -urgent diagnosis and management are essential.
The features of the history could be due to pericardial effusion or pulmonary embolism (PE) (both increased risk with SLE). Thenormal oxygen saturations and slightly enlarged heart point away from PE, and make pericardial effusion more likely. We are not toldif pulsus paradoxus is present.
Cardiac examination can be normal with a pericardial effusion. An urgent echo will exclude a signiﬁcant pericardial effusion. It willalso provide information on evidence of tamponade physiology.
It is rare to diagnose PE with an echo, but it is useful in detecting right heart dilatation/impairment and pulmonary hypertensionwhich can be strongly suggestive of a diagnosis of PE.
Therefore, from this list, an urgent echo is the most appropriate. A computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) would ruleout PE and could demonstrate an effusion, but would not reveal tamponade changes.

Whilst cooking breakfast he had become dizzy and collapsed to the ﬂoor. He lost consciousness for 20 seconds. His wife called theambulance. On arrival his GCS was 15/15, pulse 37 regular, BP 105/60 mmHg.
On arrival at the Emergency department he started to feel dizzy and his BP dropped to 92/65 mmHg. His pulse was 35 BPM and regular. AnECG demonstrated a narrow complex regular bradycardia with no P waves visible.
The Emergency department doctor administered 500 micrograms of atropine with no improvement. He remained alert and orientated. he had a large, well healed sternotomy scar and was on powerful immunosuppressants, his wife informs you he had a cardiac transplant threeyears previously.
You called the cardiology registrar who was busy for another 15 minutes with a primary PCI call.

Repeated doses of atropine at 500 mcg per dose
explanation:
This question is designed to test knowledge of the management of bradycardias.
The scenario describes a typical history of a syncopal event secondary to a bradycardia. The key to its management is therecognition of any adverse factors (shock, syncope, heart failure or ischaemia). A 30-year-old lady was found to be hypertensive during her ﬁrst pregnancy. At 32 weeks gestation her blood pressure was 155/108 mmHg.Two weeks later, the readings were 159/109 mmHg and 150/100 mmHg.
The pregnancy was otherwise uncomplicated and she had no proteinuria at any stage. There is no other medical history and she is not onany regular medications apart from folic acid.
You review her at 34 weeks gestation. Which medication should be started ﬁrst?
explanation:
Gestational hypertension with moderate hypertension is managed ﬁrst line with oral labetalol.
Gestational hypertension:Mild hypertension (BP 140/90-149/99 mmHg)Moderate hypertension (BP 150/100-159/109 mmHg)Severe hypertension (BP ≥ 160/110 mmHg)
Moderate hypertension (BP 150/100-159/109 mmHg):Treat with ﬁrst line oral labetalol (or methyldopa, nifedipine) to keep BP <150/80-100 mmHgMeasure BP at least twice a weekTest for proteinuria at each visit using an automated reagent-strip reading device or urinary protein:creatinine ratioTest kidney function, electrolytes, FBC, transaminases, bilirubin.
Reference:

A 36-year-old man is admitted to the high-dependency unit with urosepsis complicating a right-sided renal stone for which he has had anephrostomy. He has no other past medical history.
Four hours after his admission he complains of palpitations. It is not associated with chest pain or dyspnea. He is clinically euvolaemic.
The results if further investigations are as follows:
12-lead ECGatrial ﬁbrillation at 170 beats per minute
ECHO good biventricular function with no structural valve abnormalities
Serum K4.5 mmol/L
Serum Mg2.5 mmol/L
What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Chemical cardioversion is preferred to DC cardioversion, as this arrhythmia is of sudden onset BUT there are no signs of cardiaccompromise. Potential anti-arrhythmic drugs include include ﬂecanide, propafenone and amiodarone.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends an initial bolus of ﬂecanide where there is no structuralcardiac valve abnormality, which has been conﬁrmed by echocardiography.
Reference:
NICE. Atrial ﬁbrillation: the management of atrial ﬁbrillation (CG180).

An 84-year-old lady is admitted to hospital following a collapse at home with transient loss of consciousness.
On examination she appears well. Her pulse is measured at 48 beats per minute with a blood pressure of 110/65 mmHg. Herelectrocardiogram on admission shows a sinus bradycardia of 45 beats per minute with no acute or ischaemic changes.
What is the most appropriate next step in her management?
options: Admit and insert a temporary pacing wire
Admit and arrange monitored telemetry with printing
Observe overnight and arrange a 24-hour tape as an outpatient
explanation:
This patient is likely to have bradycardia-induced syncope. The diagnosis is however not certain. Therefore observation as aninpatient with suitable heart rate monitoring is the best answer.
Outpatient observation is not appropriate given the syncopal episode.
Although this patient is likely to require a permanent pacemaker at some stage, emergency temporary wire is not indicated unlesspatient has recurrent syncope due to bradycardia or complete heart block. Because the patient is cardiovascularly stable atemporary wire, atropine or carotid sinus massage are not required.

A 79-year-old lady presents to the Emergency department with fast atrial ﬁbrillation and dyspnoea.
She had a VVI permanent pacemaker implanted one year previously for sick sinus syndrome after she presented with syncope. She isadequately anticoagulated and is referred for DC cardioversion.

options: She should be treated with antiarrhythmic therapy and the cardioversion should be cancelled
Pacemaker function should be checked after cardioversion and antiarrhythmic therapy added
Her VVI pacemaker should be upgraded to a dual chamber system
Cardioversion will not affect her pacemaker

explanation:
This lady has sick sinus syndrome (tachy-brady syndrome). She has a VVI pacemaker in situ to prevent bradycardia-induced syncopebut she has presented with symptomatic fast AF.
The aim for treatment is initially to cardiovert this patient. DC cardioversion is not contraindicated in patients with pacemakers,although it is prudent to have the pacemaker function and settings rechecked after cardioversion.
Subsequently the patient should be treated with antiarrhythmic medication to prevent recurrences of fast AF.
Dual chamber pacing would not prevent AF in this case.

explanation:
The commonest cause of a mild hypertriglyceridaemia is obesity secondary to a reduced eﬃcacy of lipoprotein lipase activity andoverproduction of VLDL.
Obesity (deﬁned as a BMI above 30) is present in approximately 20% of subjects in the UK and rising, hence why it is the commonestcause of hyperlipidaemia. Alcohol is potentially the second largest cause. 
Other secondary causes of hypertriglyceridaemia include:pregnancyhypothyroidismdiuretics, andpancreatitis.

A 78-year-old female patient is under the care of your supervising consultant on the coronary care unit.
She was admitted 24 hours ago with an acute anterior myocardial infarction. She underwent a primary percutaneous intervention with agood initial result. Post percutaneous coronary intervention the patient has remained haemodynamically stable.
However, the CCU sister calls you to see the patient as she noticed the heart rate was "slow" on the monitor. The patient had started to feellight headed and her blood pressure was 105/60 mmHg.
A 12 lead ECG reveals a bradycardia with a rate of 46 beats per minute with narrow QRS morphology. There are some non-conducted Pwaves and you note the PR remains unchanged prior to the non-conducted beat.
From the list below, which is the most appropriate next management step?
explanation:
The ECG ﬁndings are consistent with Mobitz type II second degree heart block.
There is a signiﬁcant risk of asystole or complete heart block so temporary cardiac pacing is indicated in the ﬁrst instance.
Mobitz type II or complete heart block does not respond to atropine. Atropine may be useful for sinus or junctional bradycardia.
Transcutaneous is the same as external pacing (via pads); it is terrible for the patient and should only be used as a holding measure inemergency. Transvenous is via the femoral or internal jugular vein.

An 83-year-old previously ﬁt and well male patient is brought to the Emergency department after feeling unwell for some time. While in thewaiting room he collapses to the ﬂoor and is unresponsive.
He is rushed to the resuscitation area and attached to a deﬁbrillator. IV access is gained and an airway secured. The monitor shows VF and heis given a shock. Chest compressions are continued and after he remains in VF. He is shocked for the second time and chest compressionscontinue for two minutes. After this, the monitor is checked and remains in VF
According the current resuscitation guidelines, what is the immediate next management step?
options: One shock and immediately restart chest compressions
explanation:
Current UK resuscitation guidelines emphasise the importance of minimising breaks in chest compressions in a cardiac arrestsituation. After each shock chest compressions should be restarted immediately before anything else is done. The rhythmassessment (and pulse check) should happen after two minutes of chest compressions. Current guidelines also recommend singleshock strategy.
Advanced life support guidelines suggest giving adrenaline every 3-5 minutes and amiodarone after 3 shocks.
The use of brief periods of echo (10 seconds) is now supported in an arrest situation (but should be performed at the end of twominutes of compressions).
Therefore the most appropriate immediate step is one shock and immediately restart chest compressions.
Reference:
Resuscitation Council (UK). Resuscitation guidelines.

stem: During examination of the cardiovascular system, which part of the JVP corresponds to opening of the tricuspid valve with right ventricularﬁlling?
explanation:
The jugular venous pulse (JVP) is a means of assessing the function of the right side of the heart. The JVP is elevated in rightventricular failure, congestive cardiac failure and superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction.
On closer inspection, the JVP can be seen to be made up of several peaks and troughs:
a: Atrial systole. The highest pressure occurs immediately before the carotid pulse. A 65-year-old lady presents with pulmonary oedema. She is morbidly obese, suffers from osteoarthritis and gout, and has type 2 diabetes.
She has been placed on a furosemide infusion to treat her symptoms. However, she is now in acute-on-chronic renal failure with a creatinine195 mmol/L (NR 44-80) and an eGFR of 28 ml/min.
Which of the following drugs is safe to continue on the drug chart?
explanation:
Insulin is the safest agent to address hyperglycaemia in renal insuﬃciency. Insulin glargine can accumulate in renal failure, however,so the dose may need to be adjusted to avoid hypoglycaemic episodes. 
Non-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, need to be stopped to avoid further renal deterioration
Metformin should be stopped with a creatinine of greater than 150 mmol/L and/or if the eGFR <30 ml/min. Metformin is alsocontraindicated in conditions predisposing to hypoxia (e.g. pulmonary oedema).
Pioglitazone is contraindicated in heart failure and should be stopped.
Saxagliptin is not recommended in patients with moderate or severe renal insuﬃciency.

stem: According to the advanced life support (ALS) algorithm for tachyarrhythmias which of the following is appropriate?
options: Slow intravenous bolus of adenosine 6 mg, then 12 mg and then 12 mg for narrow complex regular tachycardia with no adverse featuresafter vagal manoeuvres have failed
Beta-blockers or diltiazem for narrow complex, irregular tachycardia with no unstable features
Intravenous magnesium (1.2-2 g) for polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (for example, torsade de pointes)
Intravenous amiodarone (900 mg) over 10-20 minutes after three unsuccessful DC cardioversions for ventricular tachycardia with apulse
Synchronised DC cardioversion for ventricular tachycardia without a pulse
explanation:
Irregular, narrow complex tachycardia is likely to be atrial ﬁbrillation and the Resuscitation Council (UK) advanced life support (ALS)guidelines recommend beta-blockers or diltiazem if there are no unstable features.
ALS recommends a rapid bolus of adenosine for regular, narrow complex tachycardia that does not respond to vagal manoeuvres.
Synchronised shocks are recommended only when a pulse is palpable.
The loading dose of amiodarone is 300 mg IV over 10-20 minutes when three direct current (DC) cardioversions fail to convertventricular tachycardia with a pulse.
Severe asthma is treated with 1.2-2 g of intravenous magnesium, whereas torsade de pointes requires 2 g IV.
Reference:
Resuscitation Council (UK). Peri-arrest arrhythmias.

He had an extensive list of current and previous medication in his wallet.
Which of these drugs are most likely to have been the cause?
explanation:
A large number of drugs have been implicated in causing long QT interval and torsade de pointes ventricular tachycardia.
Digoxin causes a shortened QT interval.
Amiloride, ramipril and spironolactone could lead to hyperkalaemia but it is hypokalaemia that is associated with torsade de pointesVT.

explanation:
Myoglobin rises ﬁrst, followed by troponins and CK-MB. The development of cardiac biomarkers, particularly for infarction, hasrevolutionised cardiology in the last 50 years and facilitated earlier interventions.
Troponins I and T come from the myoﬁbrils and form a troponin complex of troponin I, T and C. Troponin I becomes abnormal fourto eight hours following onset of chest pain, peaks at 12-16 hours, and remains elevated for ﬁve to nine days following an infarction.
CK-MB is elevated in MI, extreme exercise, polymyositis, chronic kidney disease and muscular dystrophy. CK-MB is more speciﬁc tomyocardium than CK-MM. Skeletal muscle however still contains some CK-MB - usually around 2% or less of total CK. Thispercentage can increase in certain muscle diseases.
BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) is produced and secreted by the atria and ventricles in response to stretch. Thus it is elevated inhypervolaemia, congestive cardiac failure and hypertension. BNP can be used in the diagnosis of cardiac failure but levels areaffected by age, sex, medications and renal function.

explanation:
The answer is A) left atrial catheter ablation.
In this situation, with three attacks of atrial ﬁbrillation over the past year, there is signiﬁcant risk of permanent AF from which it ismuch harder to achieve successful ablation. Given beta blockers and ﬂecainide are unsuitable or not tolerated, left atrial catheterablation to attain permanent sinus rhythm is recommended. This is supported by current NICE guidance.
Oral digoxin has no value in the management of paroxysmal AF, although it may be considered for patients with chronic AF whorequire rate control. Propafenone could be an option for maintenance of sinus rhythm, although bearing in mind the patient failedto tolerate ﬂecanide, it is unlikely they would tolerate propafenone.

A 75-year-old man with a known history of ischaemic heart disease is having a general anaesthetic for an inguinal hernia repair.
Following surgery the patient complains of chest pain. A 12-lead ECG shows ST segment elevation in chest leads V2, V3 and V4.
Which biochemical investigation is the most appropriate to conﬁrm a diagnosis of myocardial infarction?
explanation:
The joint ESC/ACCF/AHA/WHF task force for the redeﬁnition of myocardial Infarction deﬁnes acute myocardial infarction asdetection of rise and/or fall of cardiac biomarkers (preferably troponin) with at least one value above the 99th centile of the upperreference limit (URL) together with evidence of myocardial ischaemia with at least one of the following:Symptoms of ischaemiaECG changes indicative of new ischaemia (new ST-T changes or new left bundle branch block, LBBB)Development of pathological Q waves in the ECG, orImaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall motion abnormality.
Perioperative myocardial infarction may sometimes be diﬃcult to diagnose because the patient is anaesthetised and hence cannotcomplain of chest pain (symptoms of ischaemia absent).
In this situation, the rise of cardiac enzymes can be a valuable diagnostic tool. Myoglobin rises in one to two hours, peaks at six toseven hours, and returns to baseline by 24 hours. For creatine kinase MB increases in plasma levels usually occur six to 12 hoursafter the onset of infarction, peak at 24 hours, and return to baseline after 36 to 72 hours.
Troponin levels begin to rise at three to 12 hours after injury and peak at 12 to 24 hours:Troponin T remains elevated for eight to 21 days, andTroponin I remains elevated for seven to 14 days.
Other markers that have been used as biomarkers for acute MI include lactate dehydrogenase, ischaemia modiﬁed albumin andaspartate aminotransferase.

A 72-year-old man is reviewed in the pre-assessment clinic. He is scheduled for a total hip replacement in a week.
The patient had a myocardial infarction seven months ago and had an angioplasty where a drug eluting stent was inserted. The patient istaking clopidogrel 75 mg and aspirin 75 mg daily.

Continue both drugs and proceed as planned
Stop the clopidogrel but continue aspirin and proceed
Stop both drugs and proceed as planned
Postpone surgery for a year from the date of insertion of the stent
explanation:
Thrombosis of a drug-eluting stent is associated with high morbidity (42%) and mortality (71%). For this reason, dual antiplatelettherapy (usually aspirin and clopidogrel) is continued for at least twelve months following the insertion of this type of stent.
The risk of stent thrombosis (ST) is increased in the perioperative setting and is associated with discontinuation of antiplatelet drugs.The risk of ST has to be balanced with the risk of bleeding because antiplatelet therapy has not been stopped. Ideally electivesurgery should be postponed for twelve months when it is considered safe to stop clopidogrel and continue with aspirin. This patientis scheduled for an elective procedure.
Multidisciplinary discussion between surgeon, anaesthetist and cardiologist on how to manage antiplatelet therapy and timing ofsurgery should always take place.

You are asked to see a 40-year-old woman who has a six week history of episodes of 'the room spinning around' lasting several seconds. It istypically most severe when she is lying on her right side with the ear down. During these episodes she also has nausea. She denies anyproblems with hearing or tinnitus.
On examination, she has a rotatory nystagmus with an onset several seconds after the sudden assumption of her head in the right lateraldecubitus position using the Hallpike manoeuvre and which resolves after a minute or so.
Repeated positioning of the head in the precipitating position results in the attenuation of the nystagmus. No other abnormalities aredetected.
Audiometry investigation showed normal hearing.
What is this patient's likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is characterised by brief episodes of severe vertigo accompanied by nausea andvomiting. Symptoms are usually most severe in the lateral decubitus position with the affected ear down.
Episodic vertigo usually lasts for several weeks and then resolves spontaneously. Hearing loss is not a feature.
In contrast to positional nystagmus from a central cause, the nystagmus in BPV exhibits latency, fatigue and habituation.
Both central (eg, brainstem or cerebellum) and peripheral vestibular lesions can cause positional nystagmus and vertigo.Centralpositional nystagmus is usually static, in that the nystagmus persists as long as the head is kept in the provoking position. Positionalvertigo due to peripheral vestibular pathology is always transient. Observations of the direction of nystagmus, as well as features oflatency and fatigability, can help conﬁrm a peripheral localization and make imaging unnecessary.

explanation:
This gentleman has ischaemic cardiomyopathy. He has presented with an out of hospital cardiac arrest successfully resuscitated.
ICD implantation is the best long term management strategy for this gentleman as there is a clear morbidity and mortality beneﬁtover and above anti-arrythmic therapy in this condition, including amiodarone.

Beta-blocker, statin and ACE inhibitor therapy all have a mortality beneﬁt in either heart failure treatment and ischaemia and maydecrease the incidence of cardiac arrests, but regardless of their usage ICD therapy is ﬁrst line treatment in this patient. They arecomplementary therapies.

A 26-year-old man presented to hospital with an eight hour history of palpitations and breathlessness at rest. There was no past history ofischaemic heart disease.
His electrocardiogram showed atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) with a ventricular rate of 140 beats per minute and his blood pressure was 126/59mmHg.
What is best pharmacological agent to use for cardioversion?
explanation:
Haemodynamically stable patients with AF can be converted to sinus rhythm with large doses of oral agents or with intravenousagents.
Large single doses of ﬂecainide (300 mg) or propafenone (450-600 mg) given orally have been shown to convert patients to sinusrhythm.
Several oral agents have been used to convert atrial ﬁbrillation of recent onset to sinus rhythm, including class IA, class IC, and classIII antiarrhythmic drugs.
The class IC agents ﬂecainide and propafenone have the advantage of acting rapidly, and their eﬃcacy in converting atrial ﬁbrillationof recent onset to sinus rhythm has been documented in several placebo-controlled trials.
Flecainide and propafenone are not used in people with known or suspected ischaemic heart disease, individuals who are already onantiarrhythmic therapy, or those with a prolonged QT interval because these agents may have pro-arrhythmic effects (torsade depointes).

A 73-year-old woman is brought to hospital in cardiac arrest. She has a history of breast cancer and coronary artery disease and was found byher husband on the ﬂoor at home.
He called the emergency services, and when the paramedics arrived the patient was unconscious with no respiratory effort or cardiacoutput. She was cannulated and intubated while automated deﬁbrillator paddles were attached. She is brought immediately to theEmergency department.
The patient is transferred onto the Emergency department trolley in the resuscitation area. The monitor is reattached and the patientremains in VF. The Emergency department nurse is providing good chest compressions.
The paramedics hand over that they have not yet administered any shocks. As the team leader, you instruct one shock to be given, afterconﬁrming the rhythm.
After the shock is given, which is the next immediate management step this resuscitation situation?
options: Start chest compressions after giving IV adrenaline
explanation:
This question tests knowledge on the current UK Resuscitation Council guidelines.
New guidelines were published in 2010 but the ALS shockable rhythm algorithms are broadly in line with the 2005 guidelines theyreplaced.
It is currently believed that the best chance of survival is with rapid deﬁbrillation (when appropriate) and minimal interruption ofchest compressions. Immediately after the ﬁrst shock (and each subsequent shock) chest compressions should be restartedimmediately and pulse and rhythm reassessed after two minutes.
Adrenaline is given after the third shock (and then every three to ﬁve minutes).
Amiodarone is given after the third shock.

A 74-year-old man is referred to hospital from his GP.
He had been treated for essential hypertension, with bendroﬂumethiazide 2.5 mg and amiloride 10 mg daily. However, a routine check of hisrenal function revealed:
Serum sodium134 mmol/L(137-144)
Serum potassium5.9 mmol/L(3.5-4.9)
Serum urea7.0 mmol/L(2.5-7.5)
Serum creatinine100 µmol/L(60-110)
When seen in the outpatient clinic, his blood pressure is 134/86 mmHg. A 12 lead electrocardiogram is normal. The GP's letter says that theamiloride was stopped the previous day.
Which of these is the most appropriate action?
options: Repeat serum urea and electrolytes (U&E) in one week
Give 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously
Give 50% dextrose with twelve units of Actrapid insulin intravenously
explanation:
Bendroﬂumethiazide, a thiazide diuretic, inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule, resulting inincreased sodium and free water clearance. A secondary effect is the loss of potassium by increased secretion in the distal tubule inresponse to the increased intraluminal sodium. Therefore, bendroﬂumethiazide may cause hypokalaemia.
Amiloride, a potassium sparing diuretic is occasionally prescribed with thiazide or loop diuretics, to prevent hypokalaemia. It inhibitsthe movement of sodium through channels towards the end of the distal tubule and collecting ducts, preventing the passage ofsodium from the urinary space into the tubular cells. This action causes hyperpolarisation of the apical plasma membrane,preventing the secretion of potassium into the collecting ducts.
Hyperkalaemia is common (more than 5%), and is unaffected by concurrent potassium depleting diuretics.
This patient has mild hyperkalaemia, with no evidence of cardiac toxicity.

A 63-year-old patient with mitral regurgitation requires an emergency non-cardiac procedure under general anaesthesia.
Which of the following perioperative goals best applies?
explanation:
Mitral regurgitation leads to a proportion of blood ejected by the left ventricle ﬂowing back into the left atrium, and thereforedilation of the left atrium and pulmonary hypertension.
Anaesthetic goals include:
Improve forward LV stroke volume and decrease regurgitant fraction. Vasodilatation can improve forward ﬂow especially ifpulmonary hypertension is a feature. Preload should be maintained or slightly increased. Decrease in afterload is beneﬁcial as longas this is not suddenly reduced
Hypoxia, hypercarbia, and high inspiratory pressures can all worsen pulmonary hypertension, and should be avoided. A slightlyincreased heart rate is preferred, as this reduces time for regurgitation as well as reducing time for excessive left-ventricular ﬁlling.High afterload would increase the degree of regurgitation.
 
Reference:
Anaesthesia UK. Valvular Heart Disease.

explanation:

If taken within one hour of presentation, activated charcoal should be tried.

The surgical registrar telephones you for medical advice regarding a 73-year-old Asian man who has presented with a sudden onset of a cold,painful, and cyanotic big toe of less than two weeks duration.
The foot itself is warm and peripheral pulses are present. The registrar suspects an arterial embolism, but is unsure about the next steps.
What should you advise him?
options: Urgent intra-venous thrombolysis and follow up in clinic
Urgent intra-arterial thrombolysis and subsequent warfarinisation
Urgent surgical revascularisation and follow up echocardiogram
explanation:
This is a case of 'blue toe syndrome', and 80% of such digital ischaemias have an emboli originating from the heart and so an urgentechocardiogram is crucial to prevent further and more severe events occurring.
Arteriography is required to detect other potential sources of embolism but not as a matter of urgency.
In a limb threatened by ischaemia urgent surgical revascularisation may be necessary and will be decided by the vascular team.Thrombolysis is an alternative to surgical intervention, in which case arterial has proven to be more successful than by theintravenous route.

A 78-year-old lady is referred for better control of her heart failure. The patient complains of increasing 'water in her legs'.
The GP letter states that this lady has congestive heart failure secondary to hypertension. She is housebound due to severe OA in her kneesand is diabetic.
A year ago she was admitted to hospital with pulmonary oedema that was successfully treated with diuretics and an increase in her ACEinhibitor dose. An attempt at further increasing ACEi resulted in a troublesome dry cough.
She is currently on the following medication: bumetanide 2 mg BD, carvedilol 25 mg BD, enalapril 10 mg BD, glibenclamide 5 mg TDS,metformin 800 mg BD, potassium chloride 600 mg tds and paracetamol PRN.
The patient denies any shortness of breath during daily activities, but sleeps on three pillows and lately has been ﬁnding it more comfortableto sleep sitting up in an armchair.
On examination her chest is clear but there is pitting oedema up to her knees. Heart sounds are normal. Investigations show normal serumurea and electrolytes.
What evidence based treatment will reduce the patient's mortality?
options: Stop potassium supplements and add spironolactone 25 mg daily
explanation:
Adding spironolactone is the most rational treatment option. This addresses both her main complaint of oedema and is proven todecrease mortality in patients with NYHA 3 or 4.
Remember that although the patient does not complain of shortness of breath, her mobility is very limited - an indication of severityof her heart failure can only be deduced from her increasingly erect posture needed to sleep.

A 73-year-old gentleman with a history of a previous myocardial infarction and longstanding hypertension presented to his generalpractitioner with a two month history of worsening exertional breathlessness.
Clinical examination revealed a resting sinus tachycardia and mild ankle oedema.
Which of the following medications will improve his symptoms and prognosis?
explanation:
The addition of an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor improves both symptoms and prognosis in this patient, whoappears to suffer from heart failure.
Digoxin helps symptomatically but not prognostically, as do the loop diuretic furosemide and the combined loop/thiazide diureticmetolazone.
Amlodipine is safe in heart failure but has no other role.

A 67-year-old man is admitted to the resuscitation room of the Emergency department with clinical evidence of an ST elevation myocardialinfarction.
Immediately following admission he has a cardiac arrest and resuscitation commenced. The initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity(PEA) but returned to a spontaneous circulation following four cycles of advanced cardiac life support. He remains sedated, intubated andventilated.
What is the next appropriate step in his management?
options: Insert a nasogastric tube and give aspirin and clopidogrel
Perform a chest x ray to conﬁrm the position of the tracheal tube
explanation:
All these options would be appropriate in the context of managing his post-arrest care.
However, the ﬁrst step should be to give aspirin and clopidogrel as this can usually be achieved quickly and easily in the resuscitationroom whilst other investigations and treatments are organised.

There is no history of chest pain, breathlessness or syncope.
An ECHO conﬁrms aortic stenosis and shows an aortic valve gradient of 40 mmHg. There is good left ventricular function.
Which of the following management options is the most appropriate choice in this case?
explanation:
Indications for surgery in aortic stenosis include a gradient of 50 mmHg or more, or associated symptoms such as syncope,breathlessness and episodes of pulmonary oedema.
This patient should be monitored in cardiology clinic so that a decision on the timing of valve surgery can be made.

A 30-year-old woman presents to the Emergency department with palpitations.There is no history of syncope or presyncope but thepalpitations can be associated with her feeling generally tired and very unwell.
Her blood pressure is 120/70 mmHg and her heart rate is 100 beats per minute and irregular. She has been having these episodes formonths. She has had three previous DC cardioversions.
She is on sotalol 80 mg twice a day and warfarin. Her echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular size and function but an enlarged leftatrial size.
What is the best long term treatment option now?
options: Refer for consideration of atrial ﬁbrillation ablation
Refer for consideration of a pacemaker
explanation:
This patient has not had anything to suggest ischaemia as an underlying precipitant for the arrythmia and therefore an angiogram orstress echocardiogram would not help.
The age of the patient also goes against the likelihood of ischaemia.
The enlarged left atrial size suggests that a repeat DC cardioversion is unlikely to work for a sustained period and two previouscardioversions have been tried.
The patient has problems with tachycardia not bradycardia and therefore a pacemaker would not be of beneﬁt.
The patient is symptomatic with the atrial ﬁbrillation and therefore should be considered for atrial ﬁbrillation ablation for a longerterm good result.

A 60-year-old woman presented with an eight week history of intermittent swelling of her tongue and face. Each episode lasted 34 hours andthen resolved spontaneously. Oral antihistamines were unhelpful.
She was diagnosed with hypertension six months previously and medication was started by her GP. There is no other relevant past medical orfamily history.
Which of the following medications is most likely to be the cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
ACE inhibitors can induce angioedema. They antagonise the ACE enzyme and therefore bradykinin is no longer degraded.Bradykinin accumulation causes angioedema. This complication appears to be more common in African-American people.
Bradykinin is a peptide that acts as a potent vasodilator and increases vascular permeability. This in turn causes rapid accumulationof ﬂuid in the interstitium. This is most apparent in the face where the skin has relatively little supporting connective tissue andoedema develops easily.
In people with ACE inhibitor angioedema the drug needs to be discontinued and an alternative treatment needs to be found, (that is,an angiotensin II receptor antagonist which has a similar mechanism but does not affect bradykinin).
Reference:1. Kostis JB, et al. Incidence and characteristics of angioedema associated with enalapril. Arch Intern Med. 2005;165:1637-42.2. Sabroe RA, Black AK. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angio-oedema. Br J Dermatol. 1997;136:153-8.

A 54-year-old obese man with a history of angina and hypertension presents with central crushing chest pain of two hours duration.
High ﬂow oxygen, sublingual GTN and aspirin are administered and venous access is obtained. Whilst being attached to an ECG monitor hecollapses, with a doctor present, and the initial rhythm is pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT). The external deﬁbrillator is located twominutes away on another ward.
Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment for this man?
options: Await arrival of deﬁbrillator, then deliver shock
He should be given a precordial thump followed by chest compressions
A ventilation to compression ratio of 30:2 should commenced
Continuous chest compressions should be started
explanation:
Guidelines from the Resuscitation Council (UK) state that if a patient has a monitored and witnessed VF/VT arrest in hospital, threequick successive (stacked) shocks should be given. Chest compressions should be started immediately after the third, with acompression to ventilation ratio of 30:2 for 2 minutes.
A precordial thump can be successful if given within seconds of the onset of a shockable rhythm. Delivery should not delay callingfor help, or accessing a deﬁbrillator, but would be indicated here whilst awaiting the deﬁbrillator. Chest compressions should startimmediately if it is unsuccessful.
Intravenous adrenaline would be given every 3-5 minutes once chest compressions had started.
Reference:
Resuscitation Council (UK). Adult Advanced Life Support.

A 22-year-old female with sinus bradycardia is seen in cardiology outpatient clinic following recurrent episodes of drowsiness, somnolenceand occasional syncope. She is scheduled for pacemaker insertion and the procedure goes ahead as planned.
Two weeks after the procedure at her outpatient follow-up she complains of persistent symptoms of dizziness and occasional palpitationswith some pulsation in the neck.
Her observations show oxygen saturations 99% on air, respiratory rate 18/min, blood pressure 80/40mmHg, heart rate 40/min regular, GCS15/15, apyrexial.
An ECG shows 1:1 AV block and bradycardia.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pacemaker syndrome or AV dyssynchronisation is a syndrome which affects people ﬁtted with a pacemaker who have inadequateAV synchronisation. There is disalignment between atrial and ventricular beats due to AV node block by inadequate pacing.
There is no encompassing diagnosing criteria but the symptoms include syncope, dizziness, hypotension and peripheral oedemasecondary to heart failure. Patients most at risk of AV dyssynchronisation are those with hypotension, low sinus rate or lowcompliance ventricles prior to insertion. ECG changes show AV dyssynchronisation with small p waves. 
Carotid artery stenosis would produce an audible bruit over the site and would not produce these ECG ﬁndings.,.The ECG ﬁndings in ﬁrst degree heart block would also differ from the above.

A 35-year-old man visits his GP after concerns regarding further invasive investigations. He had a tissue aortic valve replacement ﬁve yearsago for infective endocarditis that failed to respond to medical therapy.
For which of the following would he require prophylactic antibiotics?
options: Upper or lower gastrointerstinal tract procedures
Gastrointestinal investigation at a site where there is suspected infection
explanation:
Antibiotic prophylaxis against infective endocarditis is not recommended for people undergoing dental procedures or for peopleundergoing non-dental procedures at the following sites:Upper and lower gastrointestinal tractGenitourinary tract; this includes urological, gynaecological and obstetric procedures, and childbirth, orUpper and lower respiratory tract; this includes ear, nose and throat procedures and bronchoscopy.
Chlorhexidine mouthwash should not be offered as prophylaxis against infective endocarditis to people at risk of infectiveendocarditis undergoing dental procedures.
Reference:
NICE. Prophylaxis against infective endocarditis (CG64).

A 42-year-old lady with a recent diagnosis of systemic sclerosis is referred to hospital with headaches and blurred vision.
She has a past medical history of asthma. On examination, her blood pressure is 230/120 mmHg, and there is bilateral papilloedema withfundal haemorrhages.
Which of the following medications should be prescribed immediately?
explanation:
This is a case of abrupt onset hypertension in sclerodema renal crisis.
A major complication of systemic sclerosis is sclerodema renal crisis. Severe and life threatening renal disease develops inapproximately 10-15% of patients. This results in abrupt onset of severe hypertension, usually with grade III or IV retinopathy,together with rapid deterioration of renal function and heart failure; haematological tests often demonstrate a thrombocytopeniaand/or microangiopathic haemolysis.
The clinical presentation is typically with the symptoms of malignant hypertension, with headaches, blurred vision, ﬁts and heartfailure.
The hypertension is usually severe, with diastolic BP over 100 mmHg. There is hypertension retinopathy.
Hypertension should be treated with an ACE inhibitor and calcium channel blockers can be added. Initial studies used the older ACEinhibitors, such as captopril, but newer agents are often preferred in modern clinical practice. Renal dialysis may be required. Whencompared with other antihypertensives, ACE inhibitors are associated with improved survival and, perhaps counter-intuitively, betterpreservation of renal function.
An excessive reduction in blood pressure or hypovolemia should be avoided because both can further diminish renal perfusion andsuperimpose acute tubular necrosis upon the lesions of systemic sclerosis. Thus, parenteral antihypertensive agents (such asintravenous nitroprusside or labetalol) should be avoided. 
Reference:1. Medscape. What Is Scleroderma Renal Crisis and How Is it Managed?

This 20-year-old man is referred to the clinic by his GP with vague chest pains.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
This picture shows tendinous xanthomata which are virtually pathognomonic of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
Tendon xanthomata commonly affect the Achilles tendons and the tendons overlying the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints in thehands. Less common sites include the extensor hallucis longus and triceps tendons. Histologically, the xanthomata consist ofaccumulations of cholesterol deep within the tendon with associated ﬁbrous tissue. The skin overlying the lesion is usually normal,although if there is inﬂammation in the tendon, there may be overlying erythema.

Examination revealed a pulse of 80 beats per minute regular and his blood pressure was 136/82 mmHg. His apex beat was diffuse in naturedisplaced to the anterior axillary line in the sixth intercostal space. Neurological examination was normal.
His ECG showed sinus rhythm with occasional ventricular extrasystoles, deep anterior Q waves and ST segment elevation throughout theanterior leads.

options: Observe in the coronary care unit
explanation:
The suggestion is that this patient has an left ventricular (LV) aneurysm associated with arrhythmias.

You are fast bleeped to the Emergency Department to assist with a blue call patient. A 65-year-old male has been admitted in extremis withshortness of breath. The CXR is consistent with a diagnosis of heart failure.
The Emergency Department has already administered furosemide 80 mg intravenously, and the patient is currently on an intravenousnitroglycerin infusion. BP is 100/70 mmHg.
Despite these measures the oxygen saturations are 88% on high ﬂow oxygen via non-rebreathe mask.
Which therapy should you institute next?
explanation:
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) is commonly used in heart failure, although there have also been trials in the successfuluse of BiPAP. The positive end expiratory pressure (PEEP) acts to recruit the alveoli and so improve gas exchange whilst decreasingthe work of breathing.
Morphine is an ungraded recommendation and is not actually included on guidelines as a drug to use in decompensated heartfailure, though it is sometimes prescribed as a means of reducing anxiety and so the work of breathing.
Inotropes such as milrinone and dobutamine can be used in cases of cardiogenic shock, where there is impaired end-organ functionin patients with advanced heart failure.
Furosemide is a loop diuretic and when administered intravenously has the added effect of venodilation, which helps to reduce pre-load in an already congested patient. The effect of the diuresis comes much later and has a modest overall contribution in managingthe symptoms of shortness of breath.
Use of beta blockers is contraindicated in the acute presentation of pulmonary oedema, particularly intravenously.

A 52-year-old male who has a ﬁve year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus is admitted to a village hospital with chest pain.
His usual drug therapy includes metformin 500 mg tds and he also takes bendroﬂumethiazide 2.5 mg daily for hypertension.
On examination, he is obese with a BMI of 32 kg/m, has a pulse of 88 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 148/92 mmHg. His ECGshows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
Rescue PCI is not available and so he receives tenecteplase and his BM glucose concentrations show values between 7-12 mmol/L. Hisplasma glucose concentration obtained from the laboratory is 10.8 mmol/L (3.0-6.0).
What is the most appropriate treatment for his glycaemic control?
options: Commence intravenous insulin infusion and stop metformin
explanation:
The Diabetes and Insulin-Glucose Infusion in Acute Myocardial Infarction (DIGAMI) study demonstrated signiﬁcant reductions inmortality in subjects with diabetes and myocardial infarction (MI) treated with IV insulin infusion (followed by three months of scinsulin) compared with conventional therapy with their oral hypoglycaemic agents.
Although DIGAMI II cast doubt on the requirement for prolonged insulin therapy, in this particular patient with an acute MI and stressinsult, the most appropriate therapy is IV insulin infusion as the initial therapy.
Clearly continuation of the metformin would not be appropriate in this context in the initial stages, due to the increased risk of lacticacidosis.
Reference:1. Malmberg K. Role of insulin-glucose infusion in outcomes after acute myocardial infarction: the diabetes and insulin-glucoseinfusion in acute myocardial infarction (DIGAMI) study. Endocr Pract. 2004;10:13-6.2. Malmberg K, Rydén L, Wedel H, et al. Intense metabolic control by means of insulin in patients with diabetes mellitus and acutemyocardial infarction (DIGAMI 2): effects on mortality and morbidity. Eur Heart J. 2005;26:650-61.

A 75-year-old man with ischaemic heart disease suffers an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest following an acute myocardial infarction.
Following emergency percutaneous angioplasty and stenting the patient is admitted to the critical care unit but is heavily reliant on highdoses of adrenaline and milrinone for inotropic support. An intra-aortic balloon pump is inserted under echocardiographic guidance.
At which point of the ECG should balloon inﬂation be timed?
explanation:
Balloon inﬂation is timed with diastole once closure of the aortic valve has occurred; this corresponds to the middle of the T wave.For blood to be ejected antegrade to perfuse the tissues and retrograde to perfuse the coronaries the aortic valve must be closedand competent.

explanation:
Ninety ﬁve per cent of patients presenting with hypertension have essential hypertension. Five per cent of patients have secondaryhypertension.
The cause of essential hypertension is multi-factorial with a combination of genetics and environmental factors that result inhypertension.
In secondary hypertension the cause is a speciﬁc abnormality in one of the organs or system of the body.

He is already on amlodipine 5 mg, which was started two weeks ago at your surgery.

options: Refer for urgent specialist care on the same day
Refer for specialist care within two weeks
explanation:
This patient has accelerated hypertension and should be urgently referred for specialist care on the same day.
According to NICE guidelines, you should refer patients to specialist care the same day if they have:Accelerated hypertension (blood pressure usually higher than 180/110 mmHg with signs of papilloedema and/or retinalhaemorrhage), orSuspected phaeochromocytoma (labile or postural hypotension, headache, palpitations, pallor and diaphoresis).
Consider the need for specialist investigations in people with signs and symptoms suggesting a secondary cause of hypertension.

A 45-year-old man with no past medical history attends the Emergency department with an episode of acute onset breathlessness and chestpain. While in the toilet in the Emergency department he collapses and is found unconscious.
He is moved immediately to the resuscitation area and advanced adult life support is started. There is no respiratory effort and the monitorshows a sinus tachycardia with no pulse palpable.
His wife attends and informs you he has recently returned from a business trip in Hong Kong and had been complaining of a painful, swollenleft leg. After 10 minutes of unsuccessful advanced life support, the patient remains in pulseless electrical activity (PEA).
For this cardiac arrest scenario, which is an appropriate next step?
options: Intravenous thrombolysis followed by CPR for 90 minutes
Intravenous thrombolysis followed by CPR for 30 minutes
Transthoracic echocardiography to image the right ventricle
explanation:
Thromboembolic disease is a potentially reversible cause of cardiac arrest.
Massive PE can lead to PEA and can be treated with thrombolysis. Thrombolysis is indicated in the cardiac arrest situation forsuspected PEs. However, it can take 90 minutes to be effective and therefore must only be used if it is appropriate to continue CPRfor this duration.
Brief echo (less than 10 seconds) is appropriate in cardiac arrest, but it is unlikely right ventricular abnormalities (which mayindirectly support the diagnosis) can be demonstrated in that brief time.
FAST scan is not speciﬁcally indicated in this scenario.
Intra-arterial thrombolysis is not indicated.

A 56-year-old gentleman with a previous history of angina underwent angioplasty and bare metal stent implantation for single vesselcoronary artery disease. Following discharge home after the procedure he was entirely asymptomatic, but over the subsequent threemonths he developed exertional chest discomfort exactly the same as his previous angina.
He was reviewed in the cardiology outpatient clinic and underwent an exercise tolerance test, during which he developed 3 mm of STsegment depression after four minutes of a standard Bruce protocol.
What is the likeliest cause for the recurrence of his symptoms?
options: In-stent re-stenosis secondary to neointimal proliferation
Intimal dissection in the coronary artery
The development of new atheroma at the stent site
explanation:
This gentleman underwent angioplasty and bare metal stent implantation for single vessel coronary artery disease ﬁve monthsbefore this presentation. In-stent re-stenosis due to neointimal proliferation is the most likely cause for his symptoms.
The development of new disease in a stented segment is therefore extremely unlikely. Intimal dissection tends to occur at the timeof the procedure and therefore presents in the post- or peri-operative period rather than after several months.
Subacute stent thrombosis occurs acutely rather than over months, and typically presents with an acute MI.
A symptomatic lesion/obstruction at another site is possible but is less likely (particularly with aggressive risk factor management)than in-stent re-stenosis secondary to neointimal proliferation. This was the Achilles' heel for bare metal stent implantation, but hasrecently been largely overcome by the implantation of drug-eluting stents.

stem: The RALES study supports the use of which of the following medications in the treatment of severe heart failure?
explanation:
The RALES study supports the use of spironolactone in patients with chronic cardiac failure.
High levels of aldosterone, independent of blood pressure, have, in rats, been seen to promote cardiac and vascular hypertrophy,remodelling and ﬁbrosis.
Patients with primary hyperaldosteronism have left ventricular hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction which is more severe than thatseen in age-, sex- and BP-matched controls.
In the RALES study, in patients with severe cardiac failure taking an ACE inhibitor and loop diuretic, spironolactone (aldosteroneantagonist) reduced mortality by 30%.
In hypertensive patients the early diagnosis of primary hyperaldosteronism is important to prevent long term cardiovasculardamage.
Primary hyperaldosteronism can be due either to an adenoma producing aldosterone or to bilateral adrenal gland hyperplasia.
Investigation is with urea and electrolytes (U&Es), aldosterone/renin ratio (ARR), abdominal CT scanning and adrenal vein sampling ifrequired.
Treatment is with aldosterone antagonists and/or surgery if feasible.
Further Reading:
Stowasser M, Gordon RD. Primary aldosteronism: from genesis to genetics. Trends Endocrinol Metab. 2003;14:310-7.

A 57-year-old man was attended the Emergency department complaining of central chest pain of one hour in duration. He described thepain as being similar in character to his previous angina pain.
He was known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, but admitted that this was poorly controlled. He had had a previous admission to hospitalwith chest pain four weeks previously and had been diagnosed as having a non-Q wave myocardial infarction (MI).
During this admission he underwent coronary revascularisation by the insertion of a drug-eluting stent to his right coronary artery (RCA) withno ill effects post-procedure. He had been taking aspirin and clopidogrel regularly since then.
On his admission to the Emergency department he was clearly in pain, his blood pressure was measured at 105/65 mmHg, pulse 120 beatsper minute. His jugular venous pressure was measured 8 cm above the sternal angle.
The ﬁrst and second heart sounds were normal, with an added third heart sound. A soft ejection systolic murmur was heard in the second leftintercostal space. Auscultation of the chest revealed ﬁne inspiratory crackles at both lung bases. There was no ankle swelling.
His ECG showed gross ST elevation (4 mm) in the inferior leads with reciprocal ST segment depression in the anterior and lateral territorieswith T wave inversion.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
The electrocardiogram fulﬁls the criteria for an acute MI in the RCA territory.
He would normally warrant thrombolysis, but this is most likely to be acute stent thrombosis and therefore he should have primaryangioplasty.

A 73-year-old man is brought to the Emergency department  in cardiac arrest. He was found by his carer unconscious on the ﬂoor.
On arrival of the paramedics he was in VF and received two shocks prior to arriving at hospital. He is intubated and has good IV access.
While in the Emergency department he has had a further ﬁve shocks at the recommended energy and the appropriate doses of adrenalineand amiodarone but despite this he remains in VF.
As part of the cardiac arrest team you are called to help. You look through his medications and ﬁnd he is on bendroﬂumethiazide.
Regarding the management of this patient's cardiac arrest, which is the next most appropriate management option?
options: Repeat dose of amiodarone, at increased dose
explanation:
Refractory VF is, of course, a worrying sign in a cardiac arrest situation.
It is worth considering other management options if repeated shocks are ineffective. Also it is always worth repeatedly reviewing the"4 Hs and 4 Ts" for any possible reversible causes.
Magnesium sulphate IV is recommended for the treatment of refractory VF, if there is anything to suggest the patient may behypomagnesaemic (such as on medications which might cause this, that is, thiazides).
There is no indication for increasing doses of adrenaline or amiodarone, or increasing shock energy.
Amiodarone can be given again but this should be at the reduced dose of 150 mg.
Lidocaine is only recommended if amiodarone is unavailable, and/or has not already been given.
Therefore the most appropriate response here is magnesium sulphate IV.

She is intubated and ventilated and an urgent CT scan of her head demonstrates diffuse cerebral oedema but no intracerebral haemorrhageor mass lesion.
What is the most appropriate drug for control of her blood pressure?
explanation:
Labetalol has both alpha- and beta-adrenoreceptor antagonistic activity and is the ﬁrst choice for hypertensive crises where theaetiology is initially unclear. Agents such as GTN which may cause cerebral vasodilation and increase intracerebral pressure shouldbe avoided.
Whilst ACE inhibitors improve prognosis and in scleroderma renal crises, they are not recommended as initial agents due to the riseof precipitous falls in blood pressure which may worsen cerebral perfusion.
Reference:
Foëx P, Sear JW. The surgical hypertensive patient. Contin Educ Anaesth Crit Care Pain. 2004;4:139-143.

In the assessment of patients with suspected heart failure an echo should be performed to investigate for valvular disease, assess ventricularfunction and exclude shunts. In certain patient groups, such as the obese, echo views are often unsatisfactory.
Which test is recommended as an alternative?
explanation:
The NICE guidelines recommend that patients with previous myocardial infarction who have suspected heart failure should bereferred for an echocardiogram and specialist review within two weeks.
The guidelines also state that in the event of poor imaging by transthoracic Doppler 2D echocardiography, the clinician shouldconsider other imaging methods, such as radionuclide angiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging or transoesophagealDoppler 2D echocardiography.
The patient should also be evaluated by ECG. A normal ECG makes LVSD unlikely (sensitivity 82-97%). Serial ECGs are useful inevolving ischaemia such as occurs in acute coronary syndromes but have little value in this context.
Electrophysiology studies are useful for complex arrhythmias but will not provide clear information about shunting, ventricularfunction and valvular disease.
Coronary angiography may highlight atherosclerotic lesions but is invasive, carries a mortality risk, and would not be that useful inpatient with non-ischaemic causes to their heart failure.
Reference:
NICE. Chronic heart failure (CG108).

A 78-year-old gentleman known to have a severe left ventricular systolic impairment undergoes a CRT implant.
He arrives back on the ward the after his procedure and is found to be hypotensive and with a HR of 70 bpm and regular. His ECG shows a leftbundle branch block (LBBB) and sinus rhythm.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
When a CRT device is implanted the left ventricular lead is inserted in the coronary sinus. To obtain access to the coronary sinus acatheter with an aggressive tip is used. There is a 1% risk of causing dissection/perforation to the coronary sinus which can lead tocardiac tamponade.
This gentleman is hypotensive but there is no tachycardia because, before being considered for CRT, all patients need to be onoptimal medical therapy such as a beta blocker. The beta blocker would prevent him from mounting a normal tachycardia responsein the event of a cardiac tamponade.
There is no history of reasons for hypovolaemia and we would expect a tachycardia. (CRT pacemakers are able to appropriatelyadjust rate for non-exercise needs)
Infection is unlikely within the ﬁrst few hours of insertion of a pacemaker.Myocardial infarction is possible, but there is no chest pain, the procedure has minimal risk of disrupting coronary arterial perfusionand there is no tachycardia response. (see above)Pneumothorax occurs in around 1 in 100 cases if subclavian approach is used. We are not told of chest pain, shortness of breath orany other signs of pneumothorax. A 36-year-old man gave a six month history of a tight burning sensation behind the sternum that was usually brought on by eating heavymeals and lying in the recumbent position. He has no dysphagia, melaena, vomiting or weight loss.
Abdominal examination, including a rectal examination, is unremarkable. He did not take any regular medication and had not been usingnon-steroidal anti-inﬂammatory agents.
On the advice of his GP he had stopped smoking and improved his diet.
What would be an appropriate next step in the management of this patient's condition?
options: Omeprazole 20 mg once daily for one month
Omeprazole 20 mg b.d., clarithromycin 500 mg b.d. and amoxicillin 1 g b.d. for one week
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and rapid urease test
explanation:
In a patient aged below 55 years the symptoms of heartburn which is exacerbated by fatty foods and the recumbent position in theabsence of alarm features such as vomiting, bleeding, anaemia, unexplained weight loss, abdominal mass, or dysphagia makes thediagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease (GORD) the most likely.
In this patient group, NICE guidelines suggest if lifestyle changes are ineffective that a one month course of a proton pump inhibitor(PPI) is given or a test and treat strategy for Helicobacter pylori is employed. If one is ineffective then the other may be tried (with useof prokinietic or H2RA in the case of use of PPI after H. pylori eradication). Urea breath testing rather than glucose breath testing isused to detect the presence of H. pylori.
There is no evidence that either oesophago-gastroduodenoscopy (OGD) or H. pylori testing is indicated in these patients.
Further Reading:
NICE. Gastro-oesophageal reﬂux disease and dyspepsia in adults: investigation and management (CG184).

A 43-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is commenced on pulsed cyclophosphamide infusions due to an exacerbation ofneuropathy. 
A day after her most recent infusion she complains of suprapubic discomfort and dysuria with a pink discolouration of her urine.  A urinedipstick demonstrates 3+ blood, 1+ leucocytes, 2+ protein and nitrites negative.
Which medication, if administered alongside cyclophosphamide, reduces the risk of this complication of therapy?
explanation:
This is the presentation of haemorrhagic cystitis. 
Presentation occurs along a spectrum of disease ranging from irritative voiding symptoms with mild haematuria to massivehaematuria with the passage of clots (which may induce clot retention).
Cyclophosphamide therapy is the most common cause of haemorrhagic cystitis.  The risk is dose related and related to productionof acrolein, a urothelial toxic metabolite.  Although the whole urothelium is at risk the bladder is most commonly affected due to thelonger contact time with the toxin.  The risk of haemorrhagic cystitis is increased in dehydrated patients. 
Mesna is a drug that reacts with acrolein both inactivating it and acting to prevent its formation.  When administered alongsideintravenous cyclophosphamide it reduces the risk of haemorrhagic cystitis.
Alum and formalin may be used as bladder irrigating agents in cases of haemorrhagic cystitis in order attempt to arresthaemorrhage from the urothelium in severe cases. 
Steroids are not used in the management of haemorrhagic cystitis and antibiotics are only indicated where there is evidence ofbacterial infection.

A 50-year-old man presents with tingling in the left upper limb. The pain originated in the neck and radiated down the left arm. He proceededto have numbness and paraesthesia in the left lower limb.
On examination he had restriction of neck movements and there was a mild wasting to be noted in the left biceps. There was inversion of thesupinator and biceps jerks. His knee jerk and ankle jerk were hyperreactive and he has a positive extensor plantar response.
He then developed paraesthesia and numbness of the right lower limb. A diagnosis of cord compression was made and he underwent asurgical decompression.
Post-surgery was complicated by septicaemia and urinary tract infection and he remained in bed for four days. He subsequently developedinability to dorsiﬂex his right foot and right big toe. There was numbness on the outside of the foot and there was decreased eversion, butinversion was normal. His reﬂexes remained as before.
What is the cause of the post operative weakness?
options: Recurrence of the original cord compression
explanation:
The commonest cause of acute foot drop after prolonged bed rest is entrapment common peroneal neuropathy at the neck ofﬁbula. Whilst it is possible for this to develop at the time of surgery, the complicated postoperative course in this gentleman is likelyto have contributed.
Typically there is weakness of ankle dorsiﬂexion, eversion, diminished sensation of the lateral aspect of leg and dorsum of foot.
The ankle reﬂex remains intact.

His father has had a similar rash since he was a teenager.
What is your ﬁrst line of treatment?
explanation:
This patient presents with typical scalp and hairline psoriasis. First line treatment would involve topical corticosteroid preparations aswell as medicated shampoos containing zinc, coal tar, salicylic acid, corticosteroids or ciclopirox.
Miconazole is an imidazole antifungal topical preparation and is indicated for superﬁcial cutaneous fungal infections.
Oral griseofulvin is indicated for tinea capitis which presents with alopecia and localised scaly patches on the scalp, associated withshort, broken hair shafts.
Oral methotrexate is indicated for moderate and severe psoriasis not responding to topical therapies.
Topical permethrin is used to treat scabies infestations. Scabies does not affect the scalp in older children and adults.

A 60-year-old lady presents to the Emergency Department at 1 am complaining of acute onset of headache, left upper and lower limbweakness, nausea, vomiting and lethargy.
Computed tomography of the head shows no intra-cranial pathology. Blood investigations show a haemoglobin of 60 g/L, a platelet count of5 × 10/L and mild renal impairment. Blood ﬁlm examination shows extensive red cell fragments and conﬁrms genuine thrombocytopenia.
What should be the immediate course of action?
options: Administer fresh frozen plasma till plasmapheresis is available
Proceed with plasmapheresis using fresh frozen plasma as plasma substitute
explanation:
The patient has severe thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), a pathology with high mortality rate unless recognizedimmediately and appropriate therapy instituted. TTP is classically described as a pentad of:MAHAthrombocytopenianeurological dysfunctionrenal impairment, andpyrexia.
However, all ﬁve are not usually present or required for diagnosis.
First line therapy is plasmapheresis with fresh frozen plasma as the plasma substitute (to replace the missing factor in TTP, calledADAMTS-13). Although fresh frozen plasma on its own and methylprednisolone, together with aspirin, are useful treatment optionsthey should in no way replace institution of plasmapheresis as soon as possible, except in centres where plasma exchange is notavailable 24/7.
Platelet transfusions are contra-indicated in TTP. The pathological basis relates to micro-thrombi formation which results inischaemia in affected blood vessels with ensuing end-organ damage (neurological, renal and cardiac).

A 23-year-old female presents with rapid distension of her abdomen. A biopsy from a abdominal mass shows a B cell lymphoblasticlymphoma with a high proliferative index.
Which of the following is the cytogenetic abnormality seen in this lymphoma?
explanation:
This lady has a high grade lymphoma which is commonly referred to as Burkitt's lymphoma.
The characteristic cytogenetic abnormality is a reciprocal translocation t(8;14) while t( 11;14) (equivalent to cyclin D1) is seen inmantle cell lymphoma and t(14;18) is seen in cases of follicular lymphoma.
Burkitt's lymphoma is treated with intensive chemotherapy.  It has high response rates and is a haematological diagnosis which mustbe reached as an emergency in view of the high cell turnover.

A 40-year-old woman was diagnosed with breast cancer two years ago. She underwent a wide local excision with axillary node samplingrevealing a grade 3, 19 mm invasive carcinoma of no speciﬁc type. ER/PR positive, Her-2 negative.
As she had one positive lymph node she underwent adjuvant treatment with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. At the end of treatment shewas commenced on adjuvant endocrine therapy for a proposed course of ﬁve years.
She presents to the DVT clinic with a tense swollen left calf, ultrasound Doppler scan reveals the presence of a below knee DVT and she iscommenced on therapeutic enoxaparin.
Which endocrine agent was this lady likely to have been prescribed?
explanation:
Tamoxifen is well known to cause an increased risk of DVT and patients must be consented for this prior to commencement oftreatment.
Of all the options, only tamoxifen is strongly associated with an increased risk of thrombosis.
Patients must be told this at the time of prescription and steps taken to minimise any other risk factors such as a sedentary lifestyleand smoking.
