A 22-year-old female presents with pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath two hours following dual chamber pacemaker insertion forsinus bradycardia. She states the pain came on quite suddenly and states that she can now feel palpitations in her chest also. The procedurewas relatively straightforward bar some added manipulation needed for placement of the ﬁnal wire.
She takes no regular medication.
Observations are as follows: respiratory rate 30/min, oxygen saturations 93% on 4l, blood pressure 90/50mmHg, apyrexial, GCS 15, bodymass index (BMI) 35.
On examination she had bilateral crackles at both bases, no added heart sounds though they are noted to be quiet, abdomen soft non-tender with no focal neurology.
An AP CXR shows a large heart with bilateral mild pleural effusions and pulmonary oedema.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The presenting features here are most suggestive of myocardial rupture, likely ventricular, leading to a pericardial effusion. Thisyoung lady is haemodynamically compromised following pacemaker insertion and is likely to develop cardiac tamponade and needsurgent intervention with pericardiocentesis. The incidence of myocardial rupture is relatively small (<1%) and can be divided intoearly or late rupture with respect to the time it occurs following procedure.
Delayed perforations are less likely to cause such acute symptoms as well as a reduced incidence of tamponade and sudden cardiacdeath. Risk factors for perforation include physician technique, patient independent factor (i.e obesity or diﬃcult anatomy) and leaddesign.

Right atrial pressure16 mmHg  (1-5 mmHg)
Pulmonary artery pressure25/0 mmHg (25/9 mmHg)

explanation:
Even though the right atrial pressure is high the pulmonary artery occlusion pressure is low with a relatively low cardiac index,suggesting the patient is hypovolaemic. A ﬂuid challenge should be performed and values re-measured to assess response.
In a ﬂuid replete patient the occlusion pressure would be higher (usually >13 mmHg), therefore if the occlusion pressure if high andcardiac index low (i.e. <2.5 L/min/m) this would be more suggestive of cardiogenic shock.
In a VSD, left to right shunting causes an increase in the SvO2.

A 73-year-old man presents with symptoms of breathlessness and clinically has mild heart failure. He is known to have chronic atrialﬁbrillation. Normally he gets breathless on mild exertion (NYHA class II). His heart rate at rest is 90 beats/minute and increases to 150beats/minute on exertion.
His current medications are aspirin 75 mg OD, enalapril 10 mg BD, verapamil 180 mg OD, digoxin 125 mcg OD. The serum digoxin level ismeasured at 1.5 nmol/ml (therapeutic range 1.0-2.6 nmol/ml).
What is the most appropriate change to his medications?
options: Switch verapamil to a beta blocker
explanation:
The diagnosis in this patient is 'heart failure' with incomplete atrial ﬁbrillation rate control. This can result in exertionalbreathlessness.
The most appropriate therapy is implementing beta blockade. This has evidence in NYHA II heart failure in terms of symptomimprovement and mortality beneﬁt. In this instance it will also improve AF rate control.
Verapamil is negatively inotropic and is deleterious in heart failure and this should be replaced.
The digoxin dose at present is adequate as judged by the plasma levels being within the therapeutic range, therefore do not needincreasing.
Increasing the enalapril would be desirable but is not the most appropriate ﬁrst step.

A 78-year-old man presents to the Emergency department with dizziness. He denies any chest pain or shortness of breath.
He currently takes 10 mg felodpine for hypertension.
Upon investigation his electrolytes are normal. His ECG shows complete heart block. He has normal thyroid function test. His Echo showssevere LV impairment.
What is the deﬁnitive management in this case?
options: Dual chamber permanent pacemaker and heart failure medication
explanation:
This patient will require a permanent pacing system. He has an incidental diagnosis of severe LV impairment. A dual chamberpacemaker will mean that he will be RV paced.
The BLOCK-HF trial showed that patients with signiﬁcantly high degree of RV pacing had an increase in mortality with a conventionalpacemaker compared to a CRT. Small studies have showed RV pacing leads to negative remodelling and deterioration in LV function.Therefore, the ESC guidelines recommend a CRT system for patients with a reduced EF who are likely to have high percentage of RVpacing.
Reference:
European Society of Cardiology. Cardiac Pacing and Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy.

A 60-year-old female patient was brought to the emergency department by paramedics following a witnessed collapse at home.
When the paramedics arrived there was no response from the patient, no pulse and no recordable blood pressure. On arrival at theEmergency department her GCS was 3/15. She had been intubated by the paramedics. She had IV access.
A deﬁbrillator was attached and she was having chest compressions. She was in VF and had had two DC shocks by the crew, at appropriateenergy levels.
As she was transferred to the Emergency department trolley, the second cycle had completed. Chest compressions were halted, no pulsewas palpable and VF was conﬁrmed on the monitor. A third shock was delivered to the patient.
What is the most appropriate immediate next action?
options: Give adrenaline 1 mg after the chest compressions have restarted
Medications are not recommended at this point in advanced life support
Give adrenaline 1 mg before the chest compressions have restarted
Give adrenaline after the next assessment of rhythm
explanation:
The Resuscitation Council (UK) guidelines on Adult Advanced Life Support emphasise the importance of minimal interruption tochest compressions. This follows an increasing body of evidence that minimal interruption of chest compressions is associated withimproved outcomes.
The guidelines recommend the ﬁrst dose of adrenaline (1 mg) after the third shock, but after chest compressions have restartedimmediately.
This differs from the 2005 guidelines which recommended administering adrenaline immediately after the third shock. This wasconsidered to introduce an extra delay in chest compressions. Although this seems a minor point, it illustrates one of the mainchanges to the new guidelines that chest compressions should be interrupted for as short a time as possible.
1 mg of adrenaline should be given after the third shock.
Although 300 mg amiodarone should be given after the third shock, it should be after adrenaline has been administered.

A 59-year-old female pub landlady presents with acute, severe lumbar back pain.
There is no history of orthopaedic problems and until this event she had been in perfect health.
The patient complains of paraesthesia in the lower limbs and on further questioning has not voided urine since the onset of the pain.
Neurological examination reveals weakness (3/5 of both lower limbs) and loss of sensation to touch in L4, L5 and S1. Vibration sensation andjoint position sensation is preserved. Reﬂexes in the ankles and knees are absent and the plantar response is equivocal.
The blood pressure is 158/68 in her left arm and 150/62 in her right, heart rate 95 bpm, temperature 36.9°C and ECG shows normal sinusrhythm with no ischaemic changes.
The remainder of the examination is normal.
Which of the following investigations will be most useful in securing a diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient has a number of features of cauda equina syndrome. There is distal weakness, with associated sensory loss. Whilstclassically patients present with a sensory level, this is variable in clinical practice.
Causes of cauda equina syndrome include herniation of a lumbar disc (at L4/L5 and L5/S1), tumour (metastases, lymphoma,primary spinal tumours), trauma and infection (epidural abscess).
Clinical presentation is varied, but can include low back pain with unilateral or bilateral lower limb motor and/or sensory abnormalityand bowel and/or bladder dysfunction with saddle and perineal anaesthesia.
MRI is the investigation of choice to conﬁrm the diagnosis and determine the level of compression and underlying cause. Delayeddiagnosis and intervention can lead to permanent neurological damage, and therefore MRI should be undertaken in a timely fashion.
Determining the presence of bowel dysfunction (with reduced anal tone and sensation) can be helpful prognostically, but does notassist with the differential diagnosis.

She also developed some mouth and vulval ulcers two weeks postpartum.
Visual acuity in the affected left eye was counting ﬁngers. Full blood picture, U&Es and coagulation screen were all within normal limits. CRPwas 28. Anti-nuclear antibody, ANA titre was 1:20.
What is the most likely cause of her left BRAO?
explanation:
Behcet's disease is an inﬂammatory condition of blood vessels of unknown aetiology. It is more common in people from the easternMediterranean and the Middle East.
The vasculitic process can affect many parts of the body including the eye, which can lead to retinal artery occlusion among otherthings.
Mouth and genital ulcers with an inﬂammatory condition in a person from the Mediterranean region should make one think ofBehcet's disease as the diagnosis.

A 76-year-old woman presents to hospital following a fall. Her family think that she has slowed down and they are concerned because ofproblems with her memory over the last few months. Her daughter tells you she has good days and bad days.
On talking to her she describes she sometimes sees visions of small children and animals, but she is not bothered by this. Her brother diedﬁve years ago following a stroke.
Addenbrooke's examination revealed problems with visuospatial ability, perception and verbal ﬂuency. Examination of her upper limbsrevealed increased tone but was otherwise unremarkable.
What is the best evidence based treatment for her dementia?
explanation:
Rivastigmine is effective in treating cognitive decline in dementia with Lewy bodies. It may be effective in reducing anxiety, apathyand hallucinations; it has been shown to be better than placebo in LBD and for hallucinations.
Donepezil and galantamine are used in the treatment of Alzheimer's dementia.
Gingko biloba is a herbal medication which has not been proven to be of beneﬁt in treatment or prevention of dementia.
Memantine is used only in moderately severe to severe Alzheimer's dementia. It is usually started at 5mg and increased in steps of5mg every week until 20mg dose. 
Further Reading:1. Cummings J, Emre M, Aarsland D, et al. Effects of rivastigmine in Alzheimer's disease patients with and without hallucinations. JAlzheimers Dis. 2010;20:301-11.2. McKeith I, Del Ser T, Spano P, et al. Eﬃcacy of rivastigmine in dementia with Lewy bodies: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled international study. Lancet. 2000;356:2031-6.

stem: In a patient with aortic stenosis, what will lead to an overestimation of the severity of the problem when assessed by echocardiography?
explanation:
An overestimation of the severity of aortic stenosis can occur due to large volumes of blood passing over the valve at high velocities,which occurs in aortic regurgitation.
Ebstein's has no relationship to pure aortic stenosis, nor does pulmonary hypertension.
Mitral disease, either in the form of regurgitation or stenosis, does not increase trans-aortic valve blood ﬂow.

stem: Aortic dissection can be associated with which of the following?
explanation:
Dissection involves a tear in an artery. The speciﬁc causes and effects are determined by the extent and location of the defect.
Complete tear:Exsanguination into body cavity or pericardium.
Partial tear going forwards along aorta:Causes strokeParaplegiaRenal failure, andLost limb pulses due to interruptions with vessels supplying brain, limbs, spine and kidneys.
Partial tear going backwards towards heart:MIAortic regurgitation, andTamponade.
Dissection can present in a similar manner to MI or sudden cardiac death and is found on post mortem examination. A 55-year-old man was admitted to hospital with a twenty four hour history of constant central chest pain radiating to his left arm.
He had a past history of hypertension and had had exertional angina for two years. His regular medication included aspirin, atenolol andenalapril.
On examination he was pale, sweaty and breathless at rest. His ECG showed anterior ST segment elevation. Thrombolysis was notadministered due to the delay in his presentation.
Four weeks later he underwent an exercise tolerance test. His resting blood pressure was 150/90 mmHg. The patient developed centralchest pain radiating to left arm after two minutes of exercise and his blood pressure at this time was measured at 110/65 mmHg.
His pre-exercise ECG showed anterior Q waves, but there were no ischaemic changes associated with his chest pain during exercise.
What should be the next step?
options: Repeat the test off all medication
Stop the exercise test and arrange a thallium exercise test
Stop the exercise test and arrange coronary angiography
Stop the exercise test and repeat again in four weeks
Encourage patient to continue on the treadmill
explanation:
A normal response to exercise includes a progressive increase in heart rate and blood pressure.
This patient has angina at very low work load and a paradoxical BP response.
Even in the absence of ST segment depression at peak exercise, these ﬁndings suggest severe coronary artery disease and suchfeatures are frequently seen in patients with left main stem stenosis.
Failure of the BP to increase, or a decrease by 15 mmHg may reﬂect a decline in ventricular function due to ischaemia.

There is a diurnal variation in presentation of myocardial ischaemia.
Which physiological process is responsible for this?
explanation:
The peak incidence of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and the peak incidence of death due to ischaemic heart diseaseboth coincide at around 8-9 am.
The early morning is associated with several physiological and haematological factors which predispose to vasospasm, infarctionand death.
There isIncreasing adrenergic activityIncreased plasma ﬁbrinogen levelsIncreased inhibition of ﬁbrinolysis andIncreased platelet adhesiveness.
Thus it is likely that a pro-thrombotic, adrenergic environment in the presence of atherosclerosis may proceed to infarction.
Interestingly, NSTEMIs are not associated with this degree of diurnal rhythm.
Precipitating factors for an infarct include:Heavy physical exertionModest physical exertionSurgical procedureRestSleepEmotional stressors.

A 56-year-old gentleman with known dilated cardiomyopathy presented with exertional breathlessness on mild exertion.
He was in chronic atrial ﬁbrillation (AF) with a ventricular rate of 76 beats per minute but there were no clinical signs of pulmonary oedema.
An echocardiogram three months previously had showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%. His medication included warfarin,perindopril 8 mg, furosemide 60 mg, and spironolactone 25 mg. He had a background of asthma since childhood.
What further measures are likely to improve his symptomatic heart failure?
options: Addition of low dose beta blocker
explanation:
The addition of digoxin in patients with symptomatic heart failure has been shown to result in an improvement in symptoms,whether they are in AF or not.
Beta-blockade is contraindicated as there is a history of longstanding asthma.
Oral nitrate alone is unlikely signiﬁcantly to improve symptoms, although a combination of oral nitrate and hydralazine has beenshown in a recent study to do so.
Increasing furosemide in the context of little ﬂuid retention is also unlikely to improve the symptoms signiﬁcantly.
Diltiazem will slow AF ventricular rates as it is negatively ionotropic.
Further Reading:1. UpToDate. Overview of the therapy of heart failure due to systolic dysfunction.2. Hunt SA, et al. 2009 focused update incorporated into the ACC/AHA 2005 Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management ofHeart Failure in Adults: a report of the American College of Cardiology Foundation/American Heart Association Task Force onPractice Guidelines: developed in collaboration with the International Society for Heart and Lung Transplantation. A 39-year-old male ex-intravenous drug user (IVDU) presents to accident and emergency (A&E) with bloody diarrhoea and cramping pains inhis legs which have been worsening for a number of weeks. Six weeks ago he said he developed back pain which he attributes to gettingolder but this has not improved. The patient is known to have intermittent claudication and a recent Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is inkeeping with severe disease.
A full body CT angiogram is performed which shows emboli in the leg and some in the mesentery, with a larger mass in the ascending aorta.
On examination, the patient has an ejection systolic murmur heard loudest at the right heart border 2nd heart border.
Observations are stable and the patient is apyrexial.
What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Embolic events secondary to intra-aortic thrombus
Massive Pulmonary embolus (PE) with secondary emboli
explanation:
This may seem a fairly straightforward question at ﬁrst but this could be a number of diagnoses. Aortic valve endocarditis is high upon the list of differentials but in the absence of pyrexia and the fact that the patient is reported to be an ex-IVDU make this less likely.
Mesenteric ischaemia would be highly likely given the presentation but the subsequent imaging makes this unlikely as theunderlying primary pathology.
A fat embolus is more common in long bone fractures and would present with skin changes.
Massive PE is also another possibility but is once again unlikely given the conclusive imaging. This makes an embolic eventsecondary to intra- aortic thrombus the most likely diagnosis. Years of damage following intravenous drug abuse could result inatherosclerosis and high susceptibility to thrombus formation. 
Further reading:
Large Free-Floating Intra-Aortic Thrombus
Intra-aortic Thrombus Producing Embolic Arterial Vascular Disease

A 76-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department after a syncopal episode at home.
He recovered spontaneously but his wife, who witnessed the episode, insisted that he go to hospital. His only recollection of the episode wasthat he suddenly felt light-headed and then he passed out. He said that the episode was not preceded by chest pain or breathlessness. he had a previous history of an anterior myocardial infarction (MI) three months previously.
On examination, he appeared well. His pulse was 80 beats per minute and regular with a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg. He had a diffuseapex beat. The heart sounds were normal with no added sounds or murmurs.
A 12-lead ECG showed ST segment elevation in leads V3 to V6 and frequent ventricular extrasystoles. A serum troponin-T, taken twelvehours after the episode, was normal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Heart failure with secondary ventricular tachycardia
Postural hypotension due to poor left ventricular function
Left ventricular aneurysm with secondary ventricular tachycardia
Intermittent complete heart block post-myocardial infarction
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this situation is left ventricular (LV) aneurysm formation with secondary ventricular tachycardia (VT).
The ECG shows ST elevation three months after an acute MI, and this is suggestive of LV aneurysm formation. The history does notsuggest heart failure with VT although this should always be considered.
An acute lateral myocardial infarction is not suggested by the history nor is intermittent complete heart block post-MI.
Postural hypotension has a different clinical presentation and is therefore not the likeliest.

On examination she has a systolic and diastolic murmur heard loudest at the upper left sternal edge.

explanation:
A VSD is a systolic murmur not a diastolic murmur as stated in the question.
Aortic regurgitation can occur less commonly.
Tricuspid and mitral stenosis are rarely associated with tetralogy of Fallot.
The most common residual lesion in repaired tetralogy of Fallot is pulmonary regurgitation.

A 28-year-old woman, who is 24 weeks pregnant with her ﬁrst child is referred to the medical assessment unit with six hour history ofpalpitations. These started suddenly and are causing the patient to feel uncomfortable. On arrival she looks anxious. Her blood pressure is125/80 mmHg. Her pulse is 140 bpm and regular.
A 12 lead ECG reveals a regular, narrow complex tachycardia, rate 140. On further questioning the patient has noticed a few brief episodes ofpalpitations over the last year.
You begin to discuss the management options and the patient becomes tearful because she is concerned about the effects on her baby.
Which is the most appropriate management plan for this patient?
options: Vagal manoeuvres followed by DC cardioversion
explanation:
This question tests knowledge of the management of tachyarrhythmia in pregnancy.
The most common tachyarrhythmias in pregnancy are AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, and the ECG described here is consistentwith that. Often pregnant patients are extremely anxious regarding the effects of medications on their babies.
As in the non-pregnant population, vagal manoeuvres should be tried ﬁrst. If these are unsuccessful, as in approximately 75% ofcases, adenosine in the next step. Adenosine is safe in pregnancy (this fact can be explained to the patient for reassurance).
Verapamil should not be used in the ﬁrst trimester.
Some beta blockers can be used in pregnancy - there is small risk of fetal bradycardia and intrauterine growth retardation.
Amiodarone should be avoided unless no alternative.

A 20-year-old man has been referred to your clinic because a ﬁrst degree relative has been diagnosed with Marfan's syndrome.
The patient you are seeing is completely asymptomatic.
What is the most important investigation to perform?
options: A chest x ray to look for a pneumothorax
An ECG to exclude delta waves or a prolongation of the QT interval
An echocardiogram to assess the size of the aortic root
A stress echocardiogram to exclude premature coronary artery disease
A creatinine kinase level to exclude a myositis
explanation:
There is no association with delta waves or prolongation of the QT interval and Marfan's syndrome so performing an ECG to excludethese would not be helpful.  Also, there is no association with premature coronary artery disease and Marfan's syndrome so a stressechocardiogram would not be helpful.
There is an association with pneumothorax but this patient is completely asymptomatic and therefore a chest x ray would not behelpful.
An echocardiogram to assess the aortic root would be helpful and enlargement of the aortic root is important to risk stratify thesepatients in terms of aortic dissection which is a serious complication.
There is no association with a myositis.
The diagnosis of Marfan's syndrome is based on clinical assessment and the Ghent criteria. Although the ﬁbrillin I gene is known tobe associated with Marfan's syndrome many patients do not have the ﬁbrillin I gene.

A 45-year-old woman presents with syncope, dizziness and lethargy for one month. Her past medical history includes asthma, COPD andbreast cancer currently on oral herceptin and a sinus bradycardia for which a pacemaker was ﬁtted eight weeks ago.
Her observations show: respiratory rate 17/min, oxygen saturations 99% on air, heart rate 60, blood pressure 89/50mmHg, apyrexial, GCS15.
A diagnosis of pacemaker syndrome is made.
What are the characteristic ECG ﬁndings associated with this syndrome?
options: Small P waves with dissociation from QRS complex
Broad QRS, Flat P waves and tall T waves
T wave inversion in anterior chest leads.
explanation:
Pacemaker syndrome or AV dyssynchronisation is a syndrome which affects people ﬁtted with a pacemaker who have inadequateAV synchronisation. There are no encompassing diagnosing criteria but the symptoms include syncope, dizziness, hypotension andperipheral oedema secondary to heart failure.
Patients most at risk of AV dyssynchonrisation are those with hypotension, low sinus rate or low compliance ventricles prior toinsertion. ECG changes show AV dyssynchronisation with small P waves. 
Treatment entails replacing the device with a dual chamber device.
The ECG changes described in option A are those of hyperkalaemia. Mobitz type 2 heart block shows intermittent non-conductive pwaves without PR elongation compared to type 1 where there is PR interval prolongation before a beat is dropped.
T wave inversion can be non-speciﬁc but when accompanied with chest pain is a sign of evolving infarction.
Further reading:
Pacemaker Syndrome

A 50-year-old gentleman presents to the Emergency department with chest pain.
His electrocardiogram (ECG) on admission shows an inferior myocardial infarction. He develops complete heart block, which is accompaniedby hypotension with a blood pressure of 90/60 mmHg.
A temporary pacing wire is inserted and his blood pressure returns to 115/75 mmHg. Four hours after insertion of the pacing wire hebecomes cold and clammy with pericarditic chest pain and his blood pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg. No crepitations are present onauscultation of lung bases. His electrocardiogram shows a paced ventricular rate of 60 beats per minute.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Ruptured chordae resulting in severe mitral regurgitation
explanation:
The likeliest diagnosis is pacing wire induced RV perforation.
The time course in this situation is vital, as this often occurs through an infarcted RV wall which is more friable and thin walled.
Reinfarction is unlikely in absence of ischaemic chest pain.
Ruptured mitral chord is can complicate an inferior MI, but there would be signs of severe pulmonary oedema secondary.
Aortic dissection is unlikely given the presentation, and the ECG conﬁrms that the temporary wire continues to pace.

The orthopaedic surgeons request a medical opinion on a 77-year-old man who is at post-operative day 10 following a total hip replacement.The patient's operation had been uncomplicated and he had been well in the post-operative period to date.
On the day of referral he had suddenly developed left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath. On examination his pulse was 120/minuteand his respiratory rate 22/minute. His chest was clear to auscultation and his heart sounds were normal. His ECG showed left bundle branchblock (LBBB).
Arterial blood gases on air:
pH 7.44 (7.36-7.44)
pO 9.5 kPa(11.3-12.6)
pCO3.4 kPa(4.7-6.0)
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a common clinical conundrum.
Despite an ECG showing LBBB, PE is the likeliest explanation for this patient's chest pain and dyspnoea. Being post-operativefollowing a total hip replacement there is a signiﬁcant risk of PE. This is backed up by the blood gases which show hypoxia andhypocapnoea (that is, he is unable to oxygenate despite good ventilation).
There are no clinical signs of either LVF or pneumonia, and the gases are not compatible with either of these options.
Fat embolus is a risk intra-operatively or in the immediate post op period, but is much less likely 10 days afterwards.
The presence of LBBB raises the possibility of MI, but it is not clear whether this conduction defect is new or old. The gases are not inkeeping with an AMI, so you have to say that PE is the most likely explanation.

Her ECG shows she is in atrial ﬁbrillation with a ventricular rate of 80 beats per minute. She has a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg.
An echocardiogram shows that the left ventricular function is well preserved. She has moderate to severe mitral stenosis. The pulmonaryartery pressure is 30 mmHg.

explanation:
This patient has moderate to severe mitral stenosis which is an indication for long term anticoagulation.
CHADS2-VASc scoring is generally used as a tool to assess need to anticoagulate a patient with AF. However, the following areconditions that, if present, may trump the decision to anticoagulate:valvular heart diseaseprior peripheral embolism, andintracardiac thrombus.

stem: Which ﬁnding, on clinical examination of the pulse, suggests a diagnosis of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM)?
options: Irregularly irregular pulse suggesting atrial ﬁbrillation
explanation:
Pulsus bisferiens - a palpable double pulse which occurs in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) or mixed aortic valvedisease. The ﬁrst beat is the percussion wave of normal systole and the second wave is formed by recoil of the vascular bed (dicroticwave).
Irregularly irregular pulse suggesting atrial ﬁbrillation - this can occur in HOCM but there are also many other causes of AF.
Pulsus alternans - beats are regular in timing but alternating weak - strong in strength. This can be due to severe LVF or as acompensatory mechanism in tachycardia.
Pulsus bigeminus - weak premature ectopic beats follow every normal beat - regularly irregular pattern.
Pulsus paradoxus - exaggeration of normal reductions in systolic blood pressure (SBP) and pulse pressure during inspiration. If theSBP falls by more than 10 mmHg this is abnormal.
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is characterised by asymmetrical interventricular septal hypertrophy causing LV outﬂowobstruction and delayed LV emptying. Around 50% of cases are sporadic; others may have affected family members.
Several different genetic defects have been identiﬁed and the exact disease presentation and life expectancy depends on themutation. Genes affected include beta-myosin, troponin T, alpha trophomyosin and myosin binding protein C, which all affect themechanism of muscular contraction in the myocardium.

On day 14 from starting chemotherapy the patient is noted to have a BP of 100/60 mmHg, a pulse rate of 120 bpm, a fever of 39°C withchills and rigors.

options: Consideration for more intensive support on ITU
Blood and urine cultures and chest radiograph, together with C-reactive protein

explanation:
This question covers the important topic of management of neutropenic sepsis.
Albeit management with ﬂuids, inotropes, culturing to discover the entity of the pathogen in every case are all important, the singlemost important intervention in neutropenic sepsis is the prompt institution of antimicrobial therapy, with broad-spectrumantimicrobials, for example, piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin.

A 35-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with a high grade fever of 38.9°C. She underwent an aortic valve replacement two years agofollowing failed medical therapy for infective endocarditis.
She has needle tracks on both forearms and there are four splinter haemorrhages on her right hand and seven splinters on the left hand. Sheis also complaining of tenderness in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen. Her urine dipstick demonstrates 4+ blood and protein. ECGshows sinus tachycardia with ﬁrst degree heart block. Blood cultures are awaited.
Which of the following statements is true?
options: Previous intravenous drug use would commonly result in coagulase negative Staphylococci-associated endocarditis
Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most common cause of prosthetic valve endocarditis at twelve months post valve surgery
ECGs should be performed daily to monitor for infections involving the aortic root/aortic valve
Patient should be apyrexial before considering any valve surgery
A normal transoesophageal echocardiogram excludes the diagnosis of infective endocarditis
explanation:
Aortic valve endocarditis can cause aortic root abscess which can cause damage to the AV node resulting in prolongation of the PRinterval on 12 lead ECG.
Early infections are usually due to Staphylococcus epidermidis (coagulase negative). IV drug abuse may lead to Staphylococcusaureus (coagulase positive) infections.
A dangerous complication of aortic valve endocarditis is an aortic root abscess. This can lead to prolongation of the PR interval dueto erosion into the adjacent AV node.
Valve surgery may be deferred until the patient is apyrexial unless there is haemodynamic compromise, larger vegetations are seenor an abscess present.
It is also important to remember that a normal echocardiogram does not exclude infective endocarditis.

explanation:

Lifestyle advice should be offered initially and then periodically to people undergoing assessment or treatment for hypertension, forexample:Ask people about their alcohol consumption and encourage them to cut down if they drink excessivelyDiscourage excessive consumption of coffee and other caffeine-rich productsEncourage people to keep their salt intake low or substitute sodium saltOffer people who smoke advice and help to stop smoking, andTell people about local initiatives (for example, run by healthcare teams or patient organisations) that provide support andpromote lifestyle change.

What treatment should be given to stop the tachyarrhythmia?
explanation:
This patient's supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) should be terminated with verapamil.
This drug is second line treatment in SVT treatment after adenosine. However in this patient, adenosine is relatively contraindicatedwith the history of asthma, as it can precipitate an attack.
Amiodarone and digoxin do not have a place for routinely terminating SVTs and lidocaine has mainly been used for treatment ofventricular tachycardias and has no effect on atrioventricular (AV) nodal conduction.
The most likely diagnosis here is an AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia, and the history of previous attacks is quite typical.

Cardiovascular risk assessment tools are all imperfect and each method tends to have particular strengths and weaknesses.
Many methods underestimate the risk associated with race, diabetes, age and family history. Patients with inherited disorders suchas familial hypercholesterolaemia will have their cardiovascular risk grossly underestimated - these patients need individualspecialist assessment.

A 23-year-old male is brought into the Emergency department (ED) by helicopter having fallen from a ship into the North Sea in winter.
He is deeply hypothermic with a core temperature of 27°C. Whilst in the ED he suffers a cardiac arrest with a rhythm of ventricular ﬁbrillation(VF). Three shocks have been given, but the patient remains in VF.
Which one of the following options is the next appropriate step in management?
options: Give amiodarone 150 mg and adrenaline (epinephrine) 0.5 mg and deﬁbrillate as required
Give amiodarone 300 mg and deﬁbrillate as required
Give amiodarone 300 mg and adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 mg and deﬁbrillate as required
Rewarm to 32°C before giving any further shocks or drugs
Give amiodarone 150 mg and deﬁbrillate as required
explanation:
Cardiac arrest in profound hypothermia has several differences from cardiac arrest in normothermic patients. Recovery with intactneurology has been reported even after very prolonged arrests, therefore resuscitation should be continued for far longer thanwould normally be considered.
Hypothermic patients do not respond well to shocks or drugs and if there is no response to the ﬁrst three shocks the patient shouldbe rewarmed to at least 32°C before any drugs or shocks are administered.
Serious consideration should be given to cardiopulmonary bypass in a patient such as this.
There is no place for 0.5 mg IV adrenaline in adult cardiac arrest. A half dose of amiodarone is indicated after the ﬁfth, not the thirdshock.
